quests.correctSentence: Swimming is my favorite hobby.
quests.contrastSentence: Swim is my favorite hobby.
quests.ruleExplanation: A gerund (-ing form) can act as the subject of a sentence, functioning like a noun: Swimming is my favorite hobby. 'Swim' alone can't be a subject on its own.
quests.nativeTip: This word acts as the subject of the sentence, like a noun.

quests.correctSentence: She's interested in learning a new language.
quests.contrastSentence: She's interested in learn a new language.
quests.ruleExplanation: Verbs following a preposition always take the gerund form: interested in learning. 'To learn' cannot follow a preposition this way.
quests.nativeTip: Verbs after a preposition like 'in' take a special form.

quests.correctSentence: — What do you do for fun? — I'm really into taking photos.
quests.contrastSentence: — What do you do for fun? — I'm really into take photos.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Into' functions as a preposition, so the following verb takes the gerund form: into taking photos, following the same rule from Question 2.
quests.nativeTip: 'Into' works like a preposition here too.

quests.correctSentence: I enjoy reading books in my free time.
quests.contrastSentence: I enjoy read books in my free time.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund: enjoy reading. This is a fixed pattern that simply needs to be memorized.
quests.nativeTip: This verb always takes the -ing form after it.

quests.correctSentence: She finished doing her homework before dinner.
quests.contrastSentence: She finished do her homework before dinner.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Finish' always takes a gerund: finished doing. Verbs like 'enjoy' and 'finish' are part of a group that never uses the infinitive form after them.
quests.nativeTip: This verb, like 'enjoy', always takes the -ing form.

quests.correctSentence: — Do you want to go out? — I'd rather avoid going in this weather.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do you want to go out? — I'd rather avoid go in this weather.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Avoid' always takes a gerund: avoid going. Like 'enjoy' and 'finish', it never pairs with 'to' + verb.
quests.nativeTip: This verb also belongs to the gerund-only group.

quests.correctSentence: I want to buy a new car next year.
quests.contrastSentence: I want buy a new car next year.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Want' is always followed by an infinitive: want to buy. This is the opposite pattern from verbs like 'enjoy', which take a gerund instead.
quests.nativeTip: This verb always takes 'to' + base verb after it.

quests.correctSentence: She decided to quit her job.
quests.contrastSentence: She decided quit her job.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Decide' always takes an infinitive: decided to quit. It belongs to the same group of verbs as 'want', 'hope', and 'plan'.
quests.nativeTip: This verb, like 'want', always takes an infinitive.

quests.correctSentence: — What are your plans? — I plan to travel abroad next summer.
quests.contrastSentence: — What are your plans? — I plan travel abroad next summer.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Plan' always takes an infinitive: plan to travel, following the same pattern practiced with 'want' and 'decide'.
quests.nativeTip: This verb also belongs to the infinitive-only group.

quests.correctSentence: I stopped drinking coffee; it was keeping me awake at night.
quests.contrastSentence: I stopped drink coffee; it was keeping me awake at night.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Stop + gerund' means ending an ongoing habit or activity: stopped drinking coffee (no longer drinks it at all).
quests.nativeTip: This means ending an ongoing habit completely.

quests.correctSentence: I stopped to drink a coffee on my way to work.
quests.contrastSentence: I stopped drink a coffee on my way to work.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Stop + infinitive' means pausing to do something else: stopped to drink coffee (paused walking in order to drink). This is a completely different meaning from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: This means pausing one activity in order to do something else.

quests.correctSentence: — Did you remember to call her? — Yes, I remember calling her yesterday.
quests.contrastSentence: — Did you remember to call her? — Yes, I remember call her yesterday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Remember + gerund' describes recalling something already done: remember calling her (recalls the memory of the call itself), unlike 'remember + infinitive', which would describe not forgetting a future task.
quests.nativeTip: This describes remembering a completed past action, not a future duty.

quests.correctSentence: I had my hair cut yesterday.
quests.contrastSentence: I had my hair cutting yesterday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Causative 'have something done' uses the past participle: had my hair cut, meaning someone else cut it, not the speaker.
quests.nativeTip: This causative structure needs the past participle, since someone else did the action.

quests.correctSentence: She's getting her car repaired tomorrow.
quests.contrastSentence: She's getting her car repair tomorrow.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Get something done' follows the same pattern as 'have something done': getting her car repaired, meaning a mechanic will do it.
quests.nativeTip: This uses the same causative pattern, with 'get' instead of 'have'.

quests.correctSentence: — Did you paint the house yourself? — No, I had it painted by professionals.
quests.contrastSentence: — Did you paint the house yourself? — No, I had it paint by professionals.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had it painted' shows someone else did the work, following the same causative pattern practiced in Questions 1 and 2.
quests.nativeTip: Someone else did the painting, matching the causative pattern.

quests.correctSentence: She said, 'I am tired.' → She said that she was tired.
quests.contrastSentence: She said, 'I am tired.' → She said that she is tired.
quests.ruleExplanation: Reported speech typically backshifts present to past: 'am' becomes 'was'. The original words change to reflect that time has passed since they were spoken.
quests.nativeTip: In reported speech, present tense usually shifts one step back into the past.

quests.correctSentence: He said, 'I will call you.' → He said that he would call me.
quests.contrastSentence: He said, 'I will call you.' → He said that he will call me.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will' backshifts to 'would' in reported speech: said he would call, following the same backshifting pattern as Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: 'Will' also shifts back one step in reported speech.

quests.conceptTitle: Reported Speech: Present Perfect to Past Perfect
quests.grammarRule: Reported Speech: Present Perfect to Past Perfect
quests.correctSentence: — What did she say? — She said she had finished the project already.
quests.contrastSentence: — What did she say? — She said she has finished the project already.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect ('has finished') backshifts to past perfect ('had finished') in reported speech, continuing the same time-shift pattern from this level.
quests.nativeTip: Present perfect also shifts back a step in reported speech.

quests.correctSentence: 'Where do you live?' → She asked me where I lived.
quests.contrastSentence: 'Where do you live?' → She asked me that I lived.
quests.ruleExplanation: Reported WH-questions keep the original question word: asked where I lived. Notice the word order also changes to statement order (I lived), not question order.
quests.nativeTip: This keeps the same question word from the original question.

quests.correctSentence: 'Are you coming?' → He asked if I was coming.
quests.contrastSentence: 'Are you coming?' → He asked if I am coming.
quests.ruleExplanation: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' (or 'whether'), and 'are' backshifts to 'was': asked if I was coming.
quests.nativeTip: This yes/no question uses 'if', and the verb needs to backshift into the past.

quests.correctSentence: — What did he ask? — He asked me what time it was .
quests.contrastSentence: — What did he ask? — He asked me what time it is .
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Is' backshifts to 'was' in this reported WH-question: asked what time it was, keeping statement word order.
quests.nativeTip: This is another WH-question needing the past tense shift.

quests.correctSentence: 'Close the door,' she said. → She told me to close the door.
quests.contrastSentence: 'Close the door,' she said. → She told me close the door.
quests.ruleExplanation: Reported commands follow the pattern 'told someone + infinitive': told me to close the door, turning the direct command into reported speech.
quests.nativeTip: Reported commands use 'told someone' followed by this special verb form.

quests.correctSentence: 'Please help me,' he said. → He asked me to help him.
quests.contrastSentence: 'Please help me,' he said. → He asked me help him.
quests.ruleExplanation: Reported requests use 'asked someone + infinitive', just like commands: asked me to help, following the same pattern from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: Reported requests follow the same pattern as reported commands, just with 'asked' instead of 'told'.

quests.correctSentence: — What did the teacher say? — She told us to be quiet during the test.
quests.contrastSentence: — What did the teacher say? — She told us be quiet during the test.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Told us to be quiet' follows the same reported command pattern practiced throughout this level: told + person + infinitive.
quests.nativeTip: This is another reported command, following the same fixed pattern.

quests.correctSentence: I enjoy visiting new places when I travel.
quests.contrastSentence: I enjoy visit new places when I travel.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Enjoy' always takes a gerund: enjoy visiting, reviewing the pattern from Level 152.
quests.nativeTip: This verb always takes the gerund form, reviewed from Level 152.

quests.correctSentence: She wants to start her own business someday.
quests.contrastSentence: She wants start her own business someday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Want' always takes an infinitive: wants to start, reviewing the pattern from Level 153.
quests.nativeTip: This verb always takes the infinitive form, reviewed from Level 153.

quests.correctSentence: — What did he tell you? — He told me to be careful on the road.
quests.contrastSentence: — What did he tell you? — He told me being careful on the road.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Told me to be careful' follows the reported command pattern practiced in Level 158: told + person + infinitive.
quests.nativeTip: This is the same reported command structure from Level 158.

quests.correctSentence: All employees are required to complete the new safety training by Friday.
quests.contrastSentence: All employees are required complete the new safety training by Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Required to' takes the infinitive: required to complete, a very common structure in official workplace communication.
quests.nativeTip: 'Required' pairs with the infinitive form, a common structure in workplace memos.

quests.correctSentence: The manager suggested moving the meeting to next week.
quests.contrastSentence: The manager suggested move the meeting to next week.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Suggest' always takes a gerund: suggested moving, joining the same group as 'enjoy', 'finish', and 'avoid' from earlier in this stage.
quests.nativeTip: This verb always takes the gerund form, like 'enjoy' and 'avoid'.

quests.conceptTitle: Reported Speech: Present Perfect to Past Perfect
quests.grammarRule: Reported Speech: Present Perfect to Past Perfect
quests.correctSentence: — What did she say about the deadline? — She said the deadline had been extended.
quests.contrastSentence: — What did she say about the deadline? — She said the deadline has been extended.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Has been extended' backshifts to 'had been extended' in reported speech, closing out the full journey through gerunds, infinitives, causatives, and reported speech covered across Levels 151 to 160.
quests.nativeTip: This closes Stage 8 with the same present-perfect-to-past-perfect shift from Level 156.
